title: War with the British, 1845
hookLine: the Khalsa army crosses the Sutlej, and battles are fought at Mudki and Ferozeshah

lines: BRITISH TROOPS AT THE RIVER TOWNS.
cards: The Sutlej again. This is the river Ranjit Singh chose as a border with the British, and kept. On one bank, the Punjab.
On the other, British India, where new regiments and guns have been arriving at the river towns. Now, on a winter's day, the Khalsa army is crossing that river with its guns and horses.
The line the old Maharaja held for so long is being stepped over.

teach.b: Histories tell how the war came from more than one side. The British had been gathering troops near the Sutlej, and in Lahore that looked like a threat. The Khalsa army, proud and restless, was ready to fight.

And Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, suggests some leaders at the court were glad to send the army against the British, hoping it would be broken. Fear, pride and plotting, all at once.

The opening battle was fought near a village called Mudki, late in the day, in dust and failing light, and the British held the field. Days later came a fiercer fight around the Sikh camp at Ferozeshah.
The Khalsa soldiers fought hard behind their guns, and British accounts admit how close their own army came to disaster.
But the Sikh army's commanders, Lal Singh and Tej Singh, made choices in those days that Sikh memory still questions, and the chance was lost. More of that tomorrow.

teach.h: FRIGHTENING NO ONE, AFRAID OF NO ONE.
teach.b: In a verse of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Ninth Guru, the wise one is described as frightening no one and afraid of no one. That's not a battle plan.
It's a way to stand inside a storm without losing your center: not ruled by fear, and not ruling others by it. The soldiers at Ferozeshah showed the fearless half.
Some at the court that sent them, as Cunningham tells it, were ruled by fear of their own army.

how: Sikhs remember the opening battles of the war with the British, including Mudki and Ferozeshah, as a time of great courage by the Khalsa soldiers and of failure by some of their commanders.

o: without fear, a word from the Mool Mantar
the courage to strike first in a fight
a soldier's oath before going into battle

games.q: the war begins — tap the pairs.
p: the opening battle, in failing light
a fierce fight around the Sikh camp

s: the war had a single, simple cause
histories tell of British troops gathering, a proud army and plotting at court.
British accounts admit how close their army came to disaster at Ferozeshah
the Khalsa soldiers fought hard behind their guns.

games.q: you're at the Lahore court. the army is restless and the British are gathering troops across the Sutlej. what do some leaders at court do, as Cunningham tells it?
o: hold the army back at any cost.
send the army against the British, hoping it will be broken.
go to the British to ask for peace.
games.why: Cunningham suggests some court leaders were glad to send the army to war, hoping to be rid of its power.

practice: Bring to mind one conflict in your life right now, and without replaying the argument, see it from a little distance, like a river you're standing beside.
Breathe in and feel your feet on the ground, breathe out and let your shoulders drop, frightening no one, not afraid. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Nirbhau, without fear. The word in the Mool Mantar, and the spirit of Guru Tegh Bahadur's verse, as the Khalsa army crosses the Sutlej to fight at Mudki and Ferozeshah.
